⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

Industry observers note that this happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

Sources indicate that A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user notes "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Industry observers note that prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt demonstrates you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

According to recent reports, before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

Industry observers note that the second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = latest LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

It has been revealed that you can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Industry observers note that plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

Industry observers note that the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

Industry observers note that one warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Recent findings suggest that free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

According to recent reports, now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

Recent findings suggest that give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Industry observers note that limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = fresh RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

Recent findings suggest that build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

#207417. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1689 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

Sources indicate that the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

According to recent reports, importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely fresh type of medical test.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," mentioned Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

According to recent reports, sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

According to recent reports, immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially crucial.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

Doctors right now rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

In a recent development, the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

It has been revealed that the researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

Sources indicate that the AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

Industry observers note that "Good AI starts with good data," noted Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Newly introduced Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most notable contributions to medicine, opening upcoming directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA VI is only right now available on the PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S, with no word yet on when a PC port will arrive. However, this has not stopped enterprising gamers and developers from working on their own PC version, especially with the release of the AI-powered Reverse Engineer Anything tool. Take-Two Interactive is not taking kindly to this, though, with VideoCardz reporting that the company has issued a DMCA takedown on 3,007 repositories on GitHub. This is the biggest action that Rockstar’s parent company has taken to protect GTA VI so far, which came just a day after a 15-year-old’s recompilation project was shut down on both Discord and GitHub.

GTA 6 on pc now runs visually identical to the consoles Vlctory emulator have loaded the full shaders of GTA 6 on pc now https://t.co/QrgoeCQ0GDNovember 25, 2026.

Despite the massive crackdown, it seems that development is simply moving away from the public platform into private spaces. PortWatch VI, a website tracking the work on unofficial GTA VI PC ports, is presently following 30 projects, with one of the more successful ones reportedly playing for over 90 minutes on an RTX 3050 GPU without any crashes, albeit at an unplayable 1 to 3 FPS. There’s also a post on the r/FitGirlRepack subreddit claiming that an unofficial port could already hit 30 FPS, with the developers working on it targeting 60 FPS within the next three days. They also expect to release the source code within the same time frame.

Porting games to other platforms used to be a difficult, time-intensive job, but the proliferation of AI tools has made it so much easier (although still requiring skill and effort). This is why one game decompilation hub froze its leaderboard, which had turned into a hollow numbers game as teams rushed to ship PC buggy or laggy PC ports. Anthropic has also taken steps to prevent Claude from being used for video game cloning and reverse-engineering, but independent developers could use other AI tools, like locally run open-weight models, to do the job for them.

There have been rumors that Rockstar will launch the game on PC as early as the first quarter of 2027, a massive improvement over the 18-month delay PC gamers had to endure with the previous installment. Rockstar’s parent company certainly wants to recoup the over $2 billion spent on developing the game, and having it available to the millions of PC gamers would certainly help with that goal. But the power that AI has given to developers to allow them to make unofficial ports much more swiftly than before is certainly adding to the pressure.

Latest Update: The most dangerous election disinformation campaigns

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up.
  • You scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up.
  • In a recent development, candidates and their supporters spent a whopping $80 million to make AI-generated ads, as part of what AdImpact projected will be the most expensive election cycle on record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up. It doesn’t matter who you planned to vote for, the video struck an emotional—and negative—response. The clip was not AI-generated; the candidate really uttered the words you found upsetting. But the story the video told was fundamentally false. That was the 2026 midterms. Candidates and their supporters spent a whopping $80 million to make AI-generated ads, as part of what AdImpact projected will be the most expensive election cycle on record. This is one attempt to capture eyeballs and sway voters. Another is through foreign interference. In just one example, researchers tracking a Russian influence operation recently found a fake video masquerading as a Mother Jones report that captured over 11 million views. But disinformation is not stopping at deepfakes. Authentic videos that are repurposed and stripped of context represent a new frontier. I am not talking about a mere twisting of words. What we’re seeing is next level. THE NEW LOOK OF DISINFORMATION Think about the recent catastrophic flooding in Nepal and India. Some footage released within hours of the floods, intended to showcase the magnitude of the disaster, turned out to be from entirely different events. The footage was authentic. It just happened to be from a glacial flood in Alaska, a landslide in Japan, or a flood that occurred years before. These videos racked up millions of views. They also caused panic among friends and relatives trying to find information about their missing loved ones, and they potentially hindered rescue efforts by confusing the locations where help was needed. Now, consider the same tactic applied in the political sphere—real speeches and words taken drastically out of context, coming from events that could have happened years earlier. One of the most notable examples involved Michigan’s recently elected Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed. In August, he was eviscerated by Republicans for apparently calling for Sharia law to take over in America. Social media went crazy. Was the clip real? Yes, it was from a speech he gave in 2022. But the meaning was quite different when you look at its entirety in context. So different that Politifact gave it a “pants on fire” rating for its meaning being distorted. In Georgia’s hotly contested Senate race, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff ran an ad of Republican Mike Collins urging Americans to get off Social Security and return to work. But that’s not exactly how it went down. The audio came from a broader conversation about tax policy, government revenue, and workforce participation. Collins was not saying retirees should get back into the workforce and lose their benefits (Politifact rated this one as “mostly false”). In both cases, the recordings were authentic. The misleading impressions came from stripping away the information necessary to understand what was being noted, not from manipulating the original material. You may believe that this is just par for the course in a political campaign, but just because something is common does not make it safe, normal, or acceptable. THE IMPORTANCE OF CONTEXTUAL UNDERSTANDING This tactic is becoming effective for two main reasons. Video is now our most prominent data source. Everything is recorded, so if someone is looking for a soundbite to make someone look bad, there is plenty of material available, if they’re willing to dig for it. The second matter is more technical. Deepfake detectors look for signs of manipulation. Authentic videos pass that test. Determining whether a clip is deliberately misleading requires a new set of inquiries, identifying when and where the video took place, what was happening around it, and what the broader context revealed. Making such determinations traditionally has taken a lot of people a lot of time to dig through archives. Even with the deep war chests candidates possess, they’re not going to devote the human resources needed to debunk every false video, at least not in time for that work to make a dent in the video’s impact. So, campaigns take hits, and candidates can spend considerable time and energy trying to explain past comments and rebuild trust. WHAT’S THE FIX? In 2026, voters and media companies are learning that two things can simultaneously be true: A clip can be legitimate while what it depicts is inaccurate. Voters are overwhelmed with election messages. Expecting them to research every clip they see is highly unlikely. Candidates and their backers count on this. Media companies and social platforms bear a greater responsibility, however. Fact-checking and moderation capabilities are essential to reduce the rapid spread of disinformation. Interestingly, while generative AI can be used to create convincing fakes, a different application of AI can be a powerful tool for identifying misleading content and stopping its spread. As good as AI is getting at generating realistic videos, it’s also getting good at understanding them. Solutions that can read a video and its contextual clues can be indispensable in determining whether an authentic video is being misrepresented online. Imagine an instant army of agent fact-checkers. When AI understands video the way a human does, it recognizes not only what is said and who’s speaking, but what else is on the screen and what the setting looks like. It can also search massive archives to see if that moment has appeared anywhere else. And, at the agent layer, tech can flag suspicious content, assembling supporting evidence and escalating cases to human reviewers in minutes. The technology that helps media companies and platforms find original footage, restore full context, and flag misleading claims will enable a faster response, not just to political ads but any sort of controversial content that might catch fire. Stopping the spread of disinformation is a perpetual problem. Thankfully, we are now building intelligent tools that can help. Jae Lee is CEO and cofounder of TwelveLabs.

Media companies and social platforms bear a greater responsibility, however. Fact-checking and moderation capabilities are essential to reduce the rapid spread of disinformation. Interestingly, while generative AI can be used to create convincing fakes, a different application of AI can be a powerful tool for identifying misleading content and stopping its spread.

Industry observers note that as good as AI is getting at generating realistic videos, it’s also getting good at understanding them. Solutions that can read a video and its contextual clues can be indispensable in determining whether an authentic video is being misrepresented online. Imagine an instant army of agent fact-checkers. When AI understands video the way a human does, it recognizes not only what is remarked and who’s speaking, but what else is on the screen and what the setting looks like. It can also search massive archives to see if that moment has appeared anywhere else. And, at the agent layer, tech can flag suspicious content, assembling supporting evidence and escalating cases to human reviewers in minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the technology that helps media companies and platforms find original footage, restore full context, and flag misleading claims will enable a faster response, not just to political ads but any sort of controversial content that might catch fire. Stopping the spread of disinformation is a perpetual problem. Thankfully, we are now building intelligent tools that can help.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Carl Pei says that Nothing currently has “tens of millions of devices in use,” and that there are substantial plans for 2027.

Industry observers note that this includes “more attention” to the US market for Nothing, with the US being Nothing’s fastest-growing market for audio devices. In 2026, Nothing rolled out its Ear (3a) earbuds, multiple CMF-branded devices, and two pairs of over-ear headphones including its high-end Headphone (1) Pro in September, all of which are sold in the US (and on sale during Black Friday).

Pei further stated that Nothing would have a more “aggressive” smartphone release schedule in 2027. Previously, it was said that Nothing would launch six new smartphones next year, following just three new smartphones in 2026.

In a recent development, pei said Nothing now has “tens of millions of devices in use” across its smartphones, earbuds and other products. The firm is also planning to devote more attention to the US market, while pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.

The tech giant said it has generated more than $2 billion in revenue since its first product release in 2022 and that the US is its fastest growing market for audio gear.

Sources indicate that nothing doesn’t have a strict schedule for upcoming product launches, but Nothing Phone (4a) debuted in March 2026, with Phone (3) launching in the Summer of the year prior. With six new devices supposedly in the works, it’s anyone’s guess as to when they might release.

Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.
  • AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.
  • This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret. This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic. Researchers interviewed 66 executives, managers, and employees at 58 of Anthropic’s corporate customers and found that many workers are reluctant to share their best AI tricks, citing reasons ranging from job security to more leisure time. The practice has frustrated managers looking to exploit AI-driven efficiencies. The report quotes one exasperated executive saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” AI hoarding is a new form of the age-old workplace phenomenon of knowledge hiding, in which employees deliberately withhold information from their coworkers to retain a competitive edge. Employees in the AI age have even more at stake: their jobs. If the trick they develop is powerful enough, they might render themselves redundant. And even for those whose jobs are secure, revealing a time-saving trick might just mean they are assigned more work. That raises a thorny question for business leaders: How do you incentivize employees to help automate their own jobs? Employers hoping to discourage AI hoarding may need to rethink how they measure and reward productivity. Otherwise, employees might realize that their most valuable professional asset is something they’re better off keeping secret.

Other notable features include a 5,000mAh battery, 68W wired charging, 15W wireless charging, a 50MP camera setup, and, as of writing, it should be due for an Android 16 upgrade.

The star of the show of the Moto G Stylus (2025) is the stylus. It boils down to this: if you want a phone that isn’t a Galaxy Ultra, then this is the only other line that makes sense for document signers.

In a recent development, however, there are better deals out there. I think the Galaxy A56, at just $299, is an incredible offer right now and way more deserving of your hard-earned cash. Even so, if you want clean software or that stylus, the Moto G Stylus (2025) at $199 is at least an option especially for a family member or a backup to your existing phone.

#207408. Latest Update: Innovation doesn’t scale on its own

Latest Update: Innovation doesn’t scale on its own

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear.
  • I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear.
  • Anyone who has spent time around young children knows the noise—the laughter, the crying, the constant motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear. Anyone who has spent time around young children knows the noise—the laughter, the crying, the constant motion. When malnutrition has reached a crisis point, that noise is gone. Children sit still in ways they aren’t supposed to. That stillness is one of the first signals something is wrong. Intervening early is critical. Health workers can use the most basic tools to measure a child’s upper arm to swiftly assess nutritional health. The intervention is surprisingly simple: providing a small packet filled with peanut paste, milk powder, and a precise blend of micronutrients. A six-week course of the packets follows and it can alter the entire trajectory of their life. Thirty years later, it remains one of the world’s most effective tools in global health. WHY PRODUCT INNOVATION ISN’T ENOUGH There’s a persistent bias toward the new in how innovation gets funded. Moonshots are celebrated and disruption gets rewarded. The assumption is that the most transformative solutions involve the most sophisticated technology. Breakthrough innovation is important, but collective expertise, commitment, and coordination are critical to scaling. Ready-to-use therapeutic food, known as RUTF, is one of these breakthrough innovations. Before it existed, treating severe acute malnutrition meant hospital stays and clinical formulas most families couldn’t access. RUTF changed the equation with a shelf-stable, portable product that didn’t require refrigeration. A caregiver could administer it at home. A health worker could distribute it in a village with no running water. Its success was never tied to a single organization. Over the past three decades, it has been adopted by governments, humanitarian organizations, and health systems around the world. For business leaders, the lesson is familiar. The challenge is rarely inventing the solution. It’s building the conditions that allow it to scale. THE OVERLOOKED NECESSITY We often think of innovation as a product challenge. Build the right solution and impact follows. But scale rarely works that way. What determines success is everything surrounding the innovation: distribution, financing, trust, incentives, and infrastructure. Getting RUTF to a child who needs it is more than a point A to point B challenge. It requires identifying malnutrition before it becomes irreversible, especially in the first 1,000 days of life. It necessitates a health worker who can make that call—and in many communities, that person isn’t a credentialed clinician. It is often a minimally compensated local community member. It requires supply chains that reach remote places where businesses don’t. It depends on coordination between governments, manufacturers, and health systems. If any one of those fails, a child goes untreated. RUTF endures because the ecosystem built around it proved strong enough to sustain it through political shifts, funding disruptions, and supply chain crises. That infrastructure is consistently underestimated and consistently underfunded. THE NEXT INNOVATION The next breakthrough for nutrition is a systems innovation—one that closes the gap between what works and what reaches people at scale. The UNICEF-led Child Nutrition Fund puts that idea into action. By bringing together government leadership, financing, and technical expertise, it helps accelerate the scale-up of proven nutrition interventions while strengthening the systems behind them. In doing so, it helps bridge critical gaps in nutrition services and supports country-led efforts to save lives, build resilience, and improve outcomes for women and children. That’s the innovation this moment requires—a smarter way to build and sustain the systems that deliver it. Don’t just back a product. Back the infrastructure that makes it possible. The right product can change a child’s life. The ecosystem is what gets it there, and scale is what reshapes the future. The leaders who understand this invest in the breakthroughs and the systems that make breakthroughs last. Michele Walsh is executive vice president and chief philanthropy officer of UNICEF USA.

  • The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few months, like clockwork, a new analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones. . .and of course, document the process for social media. The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling. Online, thousands of people have proudly shared their “stacks”. One popular creator, Mandy Rulez, regularly shares timelapse videos of her brain stacks before work, starting her morning with nearby stacks of non-digital activities, like journaling, before moving on to a sudoku, a crossword, and finally a quick ten pages of reading. Other creators are also incorporating timers into the mix. For example, a 12-minute brain dump in a spiral notebook, followed by ten minutes of planning, 15 minutes of puzzles, 20 minutes of coloring. Total brain stack: one hour. Brain stacking is a continuation of the “analog bag” trend earlier this year (otherwise known as, well, simply “doing things.”) But we’re in an era when “brain rot” and “doomscrolling” have become part of our everyday lexicon, so it’s easy to see the appeal. Gen Z, after all, are the ones embracing dumb phones and buying up Bricks in an effort to reduce their screen time. The idea of “habit stacking” has existed in the world of self-help for years, and involves stacking new habits to existing ones. More recently, bedtime stacking, as well as peptide stacking, have emerged as online trends. Then there’s goal stacking and income stacking. Clearly, queuing up back-to-back activities (and, ideally, literally and physically stacking them in a pile to work through) resonates with people on social media. In a year where “maxxing” was crowned Dictionary.com’s word of the year, it’s unsurprising that a single activity alone is not enough—instead, we must stack them one on top of each other to reach our max potential. (There is also the visually pleasing element of the stack when it comes to posting online.)  That does not mean there’s anything inherently wrong with brain stacking. Having a range of activities close at hand means you are far more likely to be intentional with your spare time. And a 2024 study found just five minutes of fiction reading can reduce stress by up to 20%, as well as sharpening concentration and problem-solving skills. Reading is also associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease. But recent findings from a collaboration among researchers at Clemson University, the Medical University of South Carolina, and Penn State found that “brain-training” activities, such as crosswords, sudoku, memory games and adult coloring books, are not equally effective for everyone. College students, for example, often show only modest benefits from such brain-training activities compared with older adults who live relatively sedentary lifestyles. There’s also no specific research that supports the brain stacking method of working your way through a queue of a certain number of tasks, or spending a specific amount of time on each. If you find yourself absorbed in a book, or reach a flow state in your writing, don’t feel bound to 10-minute sprints and then moving onto the next brain-boosting activity. That stated? Any amount of time away from your screens is time well spent.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the fact that high-end Nvidia AI cards reach China despite the U.S.
  • The Post details how one of its correspondents went to the Huaqiangbei market in the Shenzhen prefecture — a location known for its variety of technological goods — to try and get some export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell cards.
  • Equivalent hardware purportedly sells for around $500,000-600,000 in the U.S., but it apparently sells easily even with the apparent 5-6x markup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the fact that high-end Nvidia AI cards reach China despite the U.S. export controls isn't so much an open secret as it is simply a pricing structure. Several write-ups have illustrated that fact in the past, but today's Washington Post chronicle details how easy it is to buy the forbidden goods in China right now, with no need for secrecy or private club passwords — just talk to the sellers who have them.

The Post details how one of its correspondents went to the Huaqiangbei market in the Shenzhen prefecture — a location known for its variety of technological goods — to try and get some export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell cards. Seemingly at the cost of only a bit of conversation, an initially reluctant seller named Wu made a few calls and eventually quoted around $3 million for an eight-GPU server with Blackwell B300 chips, the highest-end version.

Equivalent hardware purportedly sells for around $500,000-600,000 in the U.S., but it apparently sells easily even with the apparent 5-6x markup. Plenty of Chinese companies are producing their own wares, yes, but at this point in time, no chip family comes close to the massive horsepower offered by Blackwell. This is a parallel story to U.S. firms, who are happy to overpay for server hardware even when the contracts they've signed change underneath them.

While inference tasks (running the models) can be performed as well or, arguably better, with efficiency-oriented alternatives, training a frontier-level model requires astounding amounts of compute power, to the tune of thousands of B300s. Hence, according to Kyle Chan from the Brookings Institution, Nvidia's wares are a 'decisive factor' in the performance-starved Chinese AI market.

A Shenzhen-based consultant put it plainly, saying that if he ever wanted to have an AI firm, he'd just go to Huaqiangbei and "work out a deal." Proving that point, the publication found more sellers dealing in Blackwell rack units, with price tags of $3-3.4 million for an eight-GPU machine.

According to seller Jason Cheng, his clients include folks from Russia and Iran, nations also covered by the U.S. AI trade export controls. The fact that those people opt to just fly to China and pay a sizable markup instead of trying to procure the GPUs more directly themselves may illustrate how well-oiled China's grey-market supply chain is. Wu told the Post he gets his cards from Hong Kong, though he's apparently unaware of where they hail from in the first place.

In a recent development, the Post raises questions about how the trade controls are taking effect, highlighting Washington's inconsistent stance on the matter, with the Treasury and the Department of Commerce seemingly at odds regarding enforcement. Heck, even procurement records for Chinese public institutions reportedly show clear purchase orders for forbidden wares.

Industry observers note that whither Nvidia in all of this? Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO despite all the controversy surrounding his relationship with a Chinese honeypot, who allegedly facilitated moving billions' worth of Blackwell GPUs to China. He's clearly stated in the past that he'd prefer the export controls gone, and that he "hopes to get more advanced chips into China." The firm has likewise repeatedly praised the U.S. government whenever it lifted an export control on its chips.

The market dip was partially a response to the Trump Administration’s overnight announcement of new tariffs, on 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Taiwan, Japan, and India despite the Supreme Court’s March ruling striking down his previous tariffs. Also rattling Wall Street: The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, which showed prices increased at a higher rate in October than expected—up 3.3%, compared with 3.1% a month earlier—leading some analysts to predict a Fed interest rate hike in December. Leading the sell-off: Nvidia. “Last week, the hope was that Nvidia could find U.S. buyers for chips that might otherwise go to Southeast Asian data centers serving Chinese customers. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies.

While both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that new models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting new safety practices while Anthropic remarked that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”.

Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work. That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations. When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t. A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption. Only 39% of people have built AI into a standardized way of working, according to the LSE Inclusion Initiative and Protiviti report. Those who have reported saving 27% of time in their work week with AI, compared with 14% for those who haven’t. Gen Z is far more likely to have been AI-trained in the past year compared with their baby boomer colleagues. AI-trained employees report saving 22% of their working hours, compared with 13% for those left to figure it out alone. And what exactly happens to all that extra time saved by AI? More time for more work, of course. And it’s causing what researchers are calling “workload creep”. “AI is creating meaningful productivity gains, but the bigger opportunity is how organizations use the capacity it creates,” said Matt Duncan, managing director at Protiviti, in the press release. “Simply absorbing those gains into existing workloads leaves much of AI’s potential untapped.” Researchers at Boston Consulting Group found that 14% of people who use AI workflows requiring a high degree of oversight experience “AI brain fry.” This mental fog and inability to focus can result in more mistakes at work, and even employees considering quitting altogether. AI or not, job performance is still dependent on people, at least for now. And the LSE and Protiviti report found no consistent association between an employee’s perceived performance and their AI adoption, access, training or workflow integration. Instead, performance stayed tied to confidence in solving problems, conscientiousness, resilience and willingness to learn. As AI continues to become embedded in everyday work, organizations need to focus on whether it is actually helping employees be more efficient at work, or simply creating time to pile more work on their plates. “Leaders should think deliberately about where that capacity can create the most value, whether that means tackling higher-value work, improving quality or giving employees greater space to solve problems and innovate,” said Duncan. “The goal shouldn’t just be doing more work faster, but using AI to change what people are able to accomplish.”.

Newly introduced workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.

As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work.

That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations.

When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it.

Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t.

A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) mentioned they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations.

While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption.

According to recent reports, only 39% of owners have built AI into a standardized way of working, according to the LSE Inclusion Initiative and Protiviti report. Those who have reported saving 27% of time in their work week with AI, compared with 14% for those who haven’t.

According to recent reports, gen Z is far more likely to have been AI-trained in the past year compared with their baby boomer colleagues. AI-trained employees report saving 22% of their working hours, compared with 13% for those left to figure it out alone.

And what exactly happens to all that extra time saved by AI? More time for more work, of course. And it’s causing what researchers are calling “workload creep”.

Industry observers note that “AI is creating meaningful productivity gains, but the bigger opportunity is how organizations use the capacity it creates,” said Matt Duncan, managing director at Protiviti, in the press release. “Simply absorbing those gains into existing workloads leaves much of AI’s potential untapped.”.

Researchers at Boston Consulting Group found that 14% of people who use AI workflows requiring a high degree of oversight experience “AI brain fry.” This mental fog and inability to focus can result in more mistakes at work, and even employees considering quitting altogether.

It has been revealed that AI or not, job performance is still dependent on people, at least for now. And the LSE and Protiviti report found no consistent association between an employee’s perceived performance and their AI adoption, access, training or workflow integration. Instead, performance stayed tied to confidence in solving problems, conscientiousness, resilience and willingness to learn.

As AI continues to become embedded in everyday work, organizations need to focus on whether it is actually helping employees be more efficient at work, or simply creating time to pile more work on their plates.

“Leaders should think deliberately about where that capacity can create the most value, whether that means tackling higher-value work, improving quality or giving employees greater space to solve problems and innovate,” said Duncan.

“The goal shouldn’t just be doing more work faster, but using AI to change what people are able to accomplish.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”?
  • “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “copilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry. “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades. Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice takes on extra weight. What is glosslighting? For the study, researchers at the university in British Columbia analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion. The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. “Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,’” the authors write. How AI jargon causes harm The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following: “Hallucination,” “copilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them. “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development. “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns. “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy. “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laypeople to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go in depth to provide greater accuracy to descriptions of AI’s impact. One author, Nicholas Vincent, an assistant professor of computing science, told Tech Xplore that “challenges where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.” “Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch update is largely focused on latest health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts.

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range.

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps users to follow their route back to a recorded point.

There’s also a new “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo.

Samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the update is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:.

The Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the revision, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

According to recent reports, A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report reveals two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

Sources indicate that A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

Recent findings suggest that this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a latest purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

It has been revealed that this separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

It has been revealed that keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

It has been revealed that providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Sources indicate that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

According to recent reports, store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Recent findings suggest that caller ID is a separate problem. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM upgrade. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.
