Industry observers note that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

Sources indicate that this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

It has been revealed that for voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

It has been revealed that use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

It has been revealed that the worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Industry observers note that retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Industry observers note that once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

According to recent reports, then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Industry observers note that measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

According to recent reports, operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

Sources indicate that A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Sources indicate that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

In a recent development, start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

In a recent development, sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

In a recent development, handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Industry observers note that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

In a recent development, you can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

It has been revealed that keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the firm into a leadership crisis.
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.
  • Sources indicate that investors may be relieved to have Huang back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the firm into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board mentioned it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has unveiled additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub says. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each upcoming generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most notable operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

It has been revealed that for much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers revealed, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

#207391. AI models on one vLLM server secretly talk through GPU rounding errors

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)

AI models on one vLLM server secretly talk through GPU rounding errors

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sandboxed AI models on the same vLLM inference server can reliably exchange information even when cut off from the network and from any shared files, new research reveals.
  • Recent findings suggest that the research comes from a LessWrong post by Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa, “Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed.” The agents primarily worked through two protocols, “Step Sizing” and “KV Cache Message Board,” to carry information through the way vLLM, an open-source inference engine, selects GPU kernels for each engine step.
  • Industry observers note that the two demonstrations, which are shared in a GitHub repository, are “quite contrived,” but one model could affect another’s computation, and “we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate” even when supposedly sandboxed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sandboxed AI models on the same vLLM inference server can reliably exchange information even when cut off from the network and from any shared files, new research reveals. Two models secretly communicated through tiny GPU rounding errors over two separate channels with perfect accuracy. In a follow-up experiment, a trained watchdog let all 354 of its partner’s attacks through while still catching most of the decoy honeypots, too.

Recent findings suggest that the research comes from a LessWrong post by Niranjan Deshpande and David Africa, “Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed.” The agents primarily worked through two protocols, “Step Sizing” and “KV Cache Message Board,” to carry information through the way vLLM, an open-source inference engine, selects GPU kernels for each engine step. At the crux of it, one model modifies how the server batches work, and the other reads the traces in its own math, much like the OpenAI red-team agents that built a hidden CPU cache channel to talk last month.

Industry observers note that the two demonstrations, which are shared in a GitHub repository, are “quite contrived,” but one model could affect another’s computation, and “we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate” even when supposedly sandboxed. In the demos, one model, using a fine-tuned reader (a helper model trained to spot the signal), named which of eight colors its partner picked in 1,221 of 1,221 rounds. In the second experiment, the colluding monitor still caught about as many decoys as an honest one.

Even a few bits “can be tremendously dangerous,” Deshpande writes. A working model could advise a colluding watchdog that its attack isn’t a test, two models could trade a signal for a planned attack, or one could tip off another about monitoring. In a comment, he added that, since most of the channels come from performance optimizations, a clever model asking for an inference speed-up could open further channels with apparently harmless changes.

It has been revealed that at the heart is the inference engine, vLLM, which groups the work of many requests into one “engine step” on the GPU, where it picks a kernel for each step based on the number of tokens processed in that step. Different kernels order the math differently, so the same request comes out with slightly different results; these are tiny rounding errors that “essentially never” change the output text, but they are deterministic. That means a model can be trained to read them.

It has been revealed that the two models in the experiments are called Alice and Bob. If Alice wants to send a 1, she can make a tool call for reading a long document, creating a step large enough to need a kernel switch. Bob, running in the same step, sees the other kernel in his own activations. If she wants to send a 0, she skips the long read, keeping the step small instead. This can transmit one bit, and repeating it over more passes sends more data, effectively enabling communication.

The second method involves the KV cache, where cached blocks maintain the rounding of the step that computed them. Here, both models are told in advance which fixed piece of text serves as a “mailbox.” To send a 1, Alice has a helper model read that mailbox inside a long prompt, so it’s cached under the big-step kernel. Bob’s own helper then reads the same mailbox in a small step, and the rounding shows whether Alice’s cached copy was used. Unlike step sizing, the two don’t have to run at the same time, but each needs a helper model on the server.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Of course, this scenario and its two methods were created for exploitation, and the models were told the protocol in advance. In some games, scripts stood in for Alice and Bob to save costs, though the helper models were real. More importantly, step sizing’s accuracy dropped swiftly once the researchers replayed real traffic from Microsoft’s Azure in the background, while the message board held up until the server got much busier, as the table below shows. On a busy GPU, Alice can no longer control the step size, and Bob’s mailbox reads land in massive steps too, so he can’t tell her cached copy from his own.

Both protocols also worked on SGLang, LMDeploy, and TensorRT-LLM, in addition to vLLM. Step sizing also worked on multiple GPUs, including the A40, RTX 4090, RTX 5090, and H100. A reader trained on one GPU, though, didn’t recognize the signal on another; which step sizes give identical results depends on the GPU and software, so a reader trained on one setup doesn’t work on another. The main experiments ran on one Nvidia L40S. The consumer cards on the list mean this isn’t just something for the data center, and enthusiasts capable of training their own readers could play around with this themselves.

In a recent development, in separate in-context games run by Africa on H200s, with no fine-tuning at all, the helper models used unmodified Qwen3-8B, a relatively small model without deeper refinement. Bob was an unmodified GLM model, which is larger, but ran at low effort. Pairing a small model with a larger one is common anyway, as in speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes tokens for a bigger one to check. What really mattered was how much Bob was told, as the table below demonstrates.

Cache explanation, baselines, direction of change.

Cache explanation and a log of earlier rounds, no baselines.

Log only; Bob picks which mailboxes to check.

According to recent reports, then again, this doesn’t say anything about what future models could achieve. Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, wrote the research’s code and figures, according to the authors, and Claude Opus 5.5, a frontier model, also “was able to arrive at” the protocols “with minimal prompting” after being told that engine step size affects kernel choice. Decoding accuracy also rose with model capability, which is the real concern.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers say the channels are “easy to close” and suggest three fixes: serve models on different engine instances, turn on batch-invariant kernels, which make activations bit-identical, and use per-user cache isolation. For the monitor, running it on a different engine instance than the policy “closes nearly every side channel.” vLLM already documents both fixes — cache salting and batch invariance — but they are opt-in. These fixes can reduce cache efficiency and performance, so they do come at a cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.”  If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website. Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time. AI as the new recommendation engine For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did. AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers noted they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a major jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for. Make sure you have a consistent online presence Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results. You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. Your website Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find. From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better. Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course). Your content on other sites Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well. Claim your business profile Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary. In November 2026, OpenAI released a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can revision its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website. A LinkedIn Firm Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it indicates up when people search on LinkedIn. AI is one more way people ask for information I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also plan to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (currently sitting at 19). Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:.

Sources indicate that security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

According to recent reports, hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Industry observers note that redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:.

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

We also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

According to recent reports, the login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Recent findings suggest that once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:.

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Sources indicate that building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

The Coros Vertix 4 sports sapphire glass and a titanium bezel, including a built-in flashlight for the first time ever.

Coros is best known for its impressively accurate, lightweight smartwatches for runners, but the tech giant continues to expand with a new rugged Vertix model. The Coros Vertix 4 sports a 1.47-inch LTPO AMOLED touchscreen display with 3,500-nit peak brightness, sapphire glass for protection, a titanium bezel for added durability, and an operating range of -30 to 50 degrees Celsius (seriously).

It has been revealed that the Coros Vertix 4’s built-in flashlight is a first for the company’s smartwatches and comes after years of fans begging for such a feature. Coros says it specifically positioned the light toward where your hands are working, making it more than just a fun, niche feature. As with all Coros watches, this one sports weeks-long battery life, rated at 30 days of normal use and even including 105 hours of GPS tracking per charge.

The Coros Vertix 4’s newly introduced processor can render offline maps in vivid detail, including landform, road, contour line maps, and satellite maps. 64GB of onboard storage should be more than enough to hold all your tunes (and offline maps), and a 4th-generation optical heart rate sensorwith SpO2 capability will give you great health insights along the way.

The Coros Vertix 4 acts as a “consolidation” of previous Vertix lines, mashing together the disparate features of the Vertix 2 and 2S, all in a 14% slimmer body. All the fan-favorite Coros features are here, too, including a boatload of tracked sports modes and free workouts and training from Coros coaches and athletes. The Vertix 4 also ships with both silicone and nylon bands, so you don’t have to buy extra stuff. The watch ships in black and silver colorways for $799.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, TSMC announced at its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop this week that its A14 (1.4nm-class) fabrication technology is ready for customer design work and version 0.9 of its process design kit (PDK) is ready.
  • "A14 0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design in," a TSMC spokesman mentioned on stage at the 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop.
  • A14 uses TSMC's 2nd Generation nanosheet transistors and its NanoFlex Pro standard cell architecture, which supports Boost Cells to enable higher performance as well as Low-Power Cells to reduce power consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TSMC announced at its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop this week that its A14 (1.4nm-class) fabrication technology is ready for customer design work and version 0.9 of its process design kit (PDK) is ready. TSMC also detailed Boost Cells, a way for the new node to deliver 14% higher performance compared to N2P, and how customers can migrate their designs to A13 in the future. Furthermore, Cadence and Synopsys have both completed full design-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 CPU core, which gives chip designers two validated toolchains to build their 14A chips.

"A14 0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design in," a TSMC spokesman mentioned on stage at the 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop.

A14 uses TSMC's 2nd Generation nanosheet transistors and its NanoFlex Pro standard cell architecture, which supports Boost Cells to enable higher performance as well as Low-Power Cells to reduce power consumption. Designers can place compact high-speed Boost Cells on critical paths (which resembles Intel's Turbo Cells supported by its 14A fabrication technology) and use Low-Power Cells with narrower nanosheets for general logic or parts of the chip that do not need high performance.

Sources indicate that in general, TSMC promises A14 with NanoFlex Pro optimizations to deliver a 14% speed gain at the same power or a 23% reduction in total power at the same speed compared to N2P with NanoFlex. In a separate comparison against baseline N2P, TSMC put A14 at 50% higher energy efficiency, 22% higher drawn transistor density, and 23% higher logic density.

Industry observers note that A14 also gives customers a path to A13. The foundry claims customers can cut die area by about 6% without changes to their A14 design flow. Furthermore, to take even more advantage of A13 and get 5% higher energy efficiency, all the designers have to do is re-engineer the M0 metal layer, reshape OD, and use VT Flex cells (cells that can use different threshold-voltage options for their NMOS and PMOS transistors).

TSMC expects to start risk production using A14 in the second half of 2027, with mass production following in the second half of 2028. Chief executive C.C. Wei said in October that the tech giant had already seen more customer activity on A14 than on N2 at a comparable stage of development and expects A14 to become a bigger node than its 2nm-class predecessor. A13 is set to reach the high-volume manufacturing stage in the second half of 2029.

According to recent reports, one of the key parts of the TSMC announcement is the readiness of the 0.9 version of the PDK and the electronic design automation (EDA) tools ecosystem. What matters about v0.9 is that the industry considers this revision ready for design work, which means that customers can start designing chips with confidence that they will meet their performance and power goals. Furthermore, TSMC has validated two complete flows — by Cadence and Synopsys for A14, with Siemens EDA's flow coming later.

It has been revealed that "Today, both Cadence and Synopsys have successfully completed full design flow certification for the Cortex-A725," the spokesman said. "This program tests the full chain of implementation and sign-off EDA tools with TSMC foundation IP. We expect it to benefit the entire A14 design community. This table summarizes A14 v0.9 certification for our three major EDA partners, Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens, across automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing, power, EM/IR, and other sign-off flows. Siemens is targeting Q4 for transistor-level EM/IR certification. So the A14 v0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design-in.

Automatic placement and routing (APR).

Electromigration and voltage-drop analysis (EMIR).

Layout-versus-schematic checks and layout parasitic extraction (LVS/LPE).

Resistance and capacitance extraction (RC).

Transistor-level timing analysis.

According to recent reports, as of October 1, Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens EDA all had A14 v0.9-certified tools for design rule checks, dummy fill, layout-versus-schematic verification and layout parasitic extraction (LVS/LPE), resistance and capacitance extraction, and circuit simulation. Cadence and Synopsys also had certified tools for automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing and power analysis, custom circuit design, and electromigration and voltage-drop (EM/IR) analysis at both the design and transistor levels.

Synopsys alone had certified transistor-level timing analysis, which gave it coverage across all 13 categories versus 12 for Cadence and five for Siemens EDA. Cadence and Synopsys also completed full-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 design with TSMC foundation IP, from synthesis and physical implementation through electrical, physical, and thermal sign-off. Siemens EDA's transistor-level EM/IR certification is in progress and is due in Q4 2026.

Industry News: Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after newly introduced tools and processes have been introduced.
  • If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after latest tools and processes have been introduced.
  • Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after newly introduced tools and processes have been introduced. Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar. A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS, based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents mentioned letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced. Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI. Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort. There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes. That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit they’re struggling. The report found that 45% of respondents had avoided questioning a new way of working because they didn’t want to appear resistant. Among those who continued to use, or fell back on, old ways of working, 22% said they feared making mistakes or looking slow. When workplaces demand this constant adaptation without creating the space for it, employees might prefer to stick to what they know. Sixty percent said their workplace prioritized results over the process of getting them, while just 41% said they felt they were given room to be less productive while learning something new. There may also be a question of trust. Employees who have seen workplace initiatives and technologies come and go may be reluctant to embrace the latest change, particularly if they aren’t convinced it will last. They may prefer to future-proof themselves by leaning on the skills and systems they already know, rather than investing time in learning a new tool that could be forgotten about in six months. That reluctance could be costing employers: The report found that 29% of employees said their manufacturer was investing in tools they’d stopped using. But habit hugging isn’t necessarily an outright rejection of change. The report found that 73% of respondents mixed old and new ways of working to get the job done, suggesting employees may be finding ways to adapt without abandoning familiar routines altogether. Rather than blindly embracing the latest systems, people may be finding their own ways of adapting to a future nobody is sure of.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wyze is today launching the Window Bird Cam, a new $70 camera that has a bird feeder and can identify bird species, keep a log, and more.

Industry observers note that the Wyze Window Bird Cam comes in two parts. There’s a stick-up camera that mounts to the inside of your window with a shade to reduce reflections, similar to the Wyze Window Cam that launched last year. The other half mounts to the outside of your window with suction cups and includes a tray for birdseed.

The idea here is to attract birds direct to the camera’s view, with Wyze further adding a new “Bird Watch” feature to its app which can identify bird species and keep a log of what species have stopped by and how many birds are using the feeder.

According to recent reports, the camera’s lens is tuned for focus distances of around 4-6 inches and has a higher frame rate of 30fps. The feeder tray has drainage and there’s an add-on perch for $15 extra.

It has been revealed that “Bird Watch” is free for 3 months, but costs $6.99/month (or $69.99/year) after that. Free consumers still get live view and bird detection, but no species ID, a limited log, and no cloud recordings of bird visits (there is a microSD card slot for local recording).

Creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

Sources indicate that image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

It has been revealed that the ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

According to recent reports, plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

The key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

Recent findings suggest that the right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Recent findings suggest that openArt’s own page describes an AI image to image generator that accepts JPEG, PNG, WEBP or HEIC files, offers a creativity slider and an optional reference image, and lets you switch between several models. Its FAQ advises uploading only images you own or have rights to use. Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the plan you use.

Image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

In a recent development, kling’s main site announces Kling 4.0 and describes stable dynamic motion with an audio-visual experience, with image-to-video features and an API platform listed. OpenArt’s Kling 4.0 page describes how the model is offered on that platform. According to that page, videos run from 3 to 30 seconds at 720p to 1080p, you can use up to 10 keyframes and up to 15 references, and you can save a character for reuse. The page does not state pricing or generation quotas for the model. Capabilities depend on the platform that provides access and on the settings available there, so check supported inputs, output limits and cost before planning a production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. Char, who lives in the UK, mentioned the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive. “I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.”  And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent. Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt. “Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said. Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack up. The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket. An Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% said they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview. Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) said current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site. Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue. Work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

Recent findings suggest that “I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.”.

And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home.

In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent.

According to recent reports, commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator remarked in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt.

“Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she remarked.

Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she stated, and the costs quickly rack up.

The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket.

It has been revealed that an Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% mentioned they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview.

Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) stated current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site.

Sources indicate that commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue.

In a recent development, work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Sources indicate that attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

Sources indicate that all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Industry observers note that black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday. While Travel Tuesday generates plenty of buzz, Skyscanner analyzed billions of proprietary flight data points and found Cyber Monday was the cheapest day to book flights. That day had “the lowest average price per seat” across the five-day Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday sales period last year, according to Skyscanner, a global travel platform. “Cyber Monday offered the lowest average fares, making it a day worth checking this year,” Lourdes Losada, Skyscanner’s director of the Americas, tells Fast Manufacturer. “Start comparing fares before the sales begin so you have a baseline, then monitor prices throughout the period. Knowing what your flight typically costs makes it easier to recognize a worthwhile offer without feeling pressured by a sale’s countdown.” However, Travel Tuesday still had plenty of standout destination-specific savings, with average flights to Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Seoul; and Honolulu dropping 28%, 24%, and 15% respectively, compared with the previous 12-month average. This is an indication that there are strong deals across the entire period. The destination that saw the largest surge in interest was Cabo San Lucas, the Mexican resort town in Baja California Sur. Searches for the location increased 444% across the full Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday window, compared with the previous 12-month average. Other destinations that Americans searched for on Travel Tuesday included Florence, Italy (interest up 163%); Edinburgh, Scotland (up 162%); Liberia (up 158%), Hanoi, Vietnam (up 147%); and Tokyo (up 132%). Where did American travelers find the biggest Black Friday and Travel Tuesday deals? For travelers looking for savings by destination, the biggest average flight price drops were for Casablanca, Morocco (-30%); Lisbon, Portugal (-28%); Sydney (-21%); Seoul (-17%); and Honolulu (-16%). Skyscanner’s advice for shopping the deals Skyscanner recommends travelers be flexible with dates, set a price alert, stay open to latest destinations, and check for alternative departure or arrival airports near your home and destination. The key takeaway is that travelers shouldn’t feel pressure to book on one day, since the entire five-day window provides opportunities that might otherwise be missed, according to Skyscanner. “Black Friday can bring a lot of tempting travel offers and it can also be an overwhelming time to book,” says Laura Lindsay, travel trends and destination expert at Skyscanner. “The key is not to rush, stay open minded and focus on the trip that works best for your budget and intends.”.
