Tech Report: The Motorola Signature 27’s haptics finally feel more like a Pixel, and it’s about time

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.
  • According to recent reports, two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on.
  • The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.

According to recent reports, two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on. It’s as gorgeous as the pictures make it look, and the texture on the back of my “Capulet Olive” green colorway is the stuff of dreams. But the thing that sealed the new ultra-high-quality design for me wasn’t the comfortable curved edges or the textile back: it was the haptic motors.

Now, don’t get me wrong. The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year. I’ll need to use it for just a bit longer to be 100% sure, but the pebble-like aesthetic of the curved front, back, and edges feels tangibly amazing to hold and use. It reminds me a bit of the Galaxy S3’s design, just without the nasty, slimy plastic back. It’s curved just enough to feel amazing, but not enough to be an annoyance like some waterfall display phones were in the past.

But a haptic motor is completely intangible to you as the reader. You can’t see it in pictures, and even if I describe it, you may not fully understand why it makes such a difference. If you’ve been using Google Pixel phones for a long time, you’ve probably forgotten how good a quality haptic motor can feel, but let me remind you for a moment just how notable such an invisible thing can be to completing the experience.

In a recent development, typing on the Signature 27 is pure bliss because of it. Tapping each key feels more like the press of a physical keyboard key. Unlocking the phone emits a satisfying light punch to my thumb, signalling a successful read. When I send a reply on X (Twitter), the button tap and subsequent animation feel like the message is being sent through the phone onto the web. It’s wonderful, and it’s one of the reasons people love the Pixel experience so much.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, the Motorola Signature 27’s haptic responses aren’t applied to as many parts of the UI as Pixel phones do, and that’s where the real miss comes in. Adjusting the brightness or volume doesn’t feel like a physically rotating vertical dial the way it does on Pixel, and I’d love to see Motorola add this in an patch. But at least the upgraded haptic engine is a huge step in the right direction for Motorola and a good way to make the Signature 27 feel like a proper flagship phone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

According to recent reports, performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

According to recent reports, how to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a fresh model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

In a recent development, eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

Measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

According to recent reports, TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Geren reopens Texas casino fight, but his amendment still needs 21 Republican-led Senate votes

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charlie Geren filed a constitutional amendment on the first filing day of Texas's 2027 session that would let voters decide on casinos and sports betting.
  • According to recent reports, texas lawmakers have their first gambling-expansion measures of the 2027 session.
  • Industry observers note that the resolution would require lawmakers to limit casinos to a capped number of facilities statewide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Charlie Geren filed a constitutional amendment on the first filing day of Texas's 2027 session that would let voters decide on casinos and sports betting. A Democratic House and a supportive lieutenant governor-elect improve its odds, but a two-thirds Senate vote and a fight over the Senate's leadership stand in the way.

According to recent reports, texas lawmakers have their first gambling-expansion measures of the 2027 session. Rep. Charlie Geren, a Fort Worth Republican, filed House Joint Resolution 52 on November 9, the first day of bill filing, and Democratic Sen. Carol Alvarado filed a Senate resolution on casinos and sports betting, SJR 11, the same day. Voters would get the final say on a constitutional change giving lawmakers the power to permit and oversee casinos and sports betting.

Industry observers note that the resolution would require lawmakers to limit casinos to a capped number of facilities statewide. Initial license terms would run at least 40 years. The Legislature would decide where sports betting could take place. The ballot wording would describe licensing, application fees and a tax on casino and sports wagering revenue at a limited number of locations.

In a recent development, geren framed a statewide vote as the end of the debate either way. A rejection at the ballot box would close the question permanently, he stated.

The political ground has moved since Geren’s last attempt. Democrats won control of the Texas House in the November 3 election. Republicans held on to the Senate. As a state representative, Goodwin backed the 2023 gambling measure. The office she won was held by Dan Patrick, who blocked gambling expansion for years.

The constitutional route keeps the bar high. An amendment needs two-thirds of both chambers, then a majority of voters. Approved amendments go on the November ballot after the session ends. In 2023, online sports betting passed the House with 101 votes. Geren’s casino resolution reached only 92. The casino measure fell short of the threshold that the betting measure cleared.

Industry observers note that the Senate is the harder test. Republicans control the chamber, and any amendment needs two-thirds support there. On November 9, Patrick urged Republican senators on conservative radio to strip Goodwin of her powers as Senate president before she takes office. Her influence over the chamber, including any gambling bill, now hangs on that fight.

Industry observers note that goodwin has signaled a conciliatory approach. Her transition team noted she wants to work with Republican senators and believes Texas is “best served by a deliberative, collaborative body.”.

Recent findings suggest that texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, arguably the casino and sports betting industry's biggest boogeyman in the Lone Star State, will leave office next year. What comes next in a crucial 2027 for the largest remaining state without major casino gaminghttps://t.co/u6WLlaAj3S.

— Ryan Butler (@butlerbetstrade) November 4, 2026.

In a recent development, industry money has struggled to change the Republican map. In the March primaries, anti-gambling incumbents beat challengers backed by the Las Vegas Sands-funded Texas Sands PAC and Texas Defense PAC, to which Miriam Adelson had given $9 million. Even so, Texas Sands PAC has pledged to keep investing in and organizing for Texas candidates who favor bringing casino gambling to the state.

That leaves Geren’s measure dependent on a Senate whose leadership is still contested. A simple majority could strip Goodwin’s powers once the chamber reconvenes in January.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss.
  • It has been revealed that bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter.
  • The pace stands out against the wider market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

It has been revealed that bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the manufacturer’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

The pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

According to recent reports, the quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

For the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

Sources indicate that A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

All third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

Industry observers note that that makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

Industry observers note that in the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

The second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the tech giant’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

Bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

— OGQ-Magazine (Online Gambling Quarterly) (@OGQMagazine) November 10, 2026.

CEO Robeson Reeves noted development projects remain on track and market conditions are stable going into the fourth quarter and 2027. The Bronx casino resort is expected to cost $4.0 billion and open by 2030. Bally’s closed a financing package led by WhiteHawk Capital Partners that provided $400 million in term loans for the project. Another $160 million in delayed-draw commitments remains available. The term loans come due 18 months after they are first funded.

The delayed third-quarter 10-Q comes next. The manufacturer has said it should arrive before its five-day SEC grace period runs out.

Building a website involves more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Developers also need to test how their code behaves in different browsers, identify layout problems, investigate JavaScript errors, and understand why certain pages take longer to load.

Sources indicate that browser developer tools make these tasks easier. They provide a way to inspect the code right now running in a browser without constantly changing files or guessing what might be wrong.

Whether you're developing a latest website or maintaining an existing application, learning to use these tools can improve your debugging workflow and help you write more reliable code.

Let's explore some useful browser development tools and how to apply them to everyday web development tasks.

Browser developer tools, commonly called DevTools, are built-in utilities available in modern browsers such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.

They allow developers to examine a webpage's HTML structure, modify CSS properties, debug JavaScript, inspect network requests, and test responsive layouts.

Recent findings suggest that you can usually open them by right-clicking a webpage and selecting Inspect. On Windows and Linux, the F12 key or Ctrl + Shift + I shortcut also opens DevTools in most browsers.

The following table highlights some commonly used features:.

Understanding what each panel does makes it easier to select the right tool for a particular problem.

The Elements panel is one of the most frequently used features in browser DevTools.

It displays the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents the structure of the webpage presently loaded in the browser. Developers can select individual elements and examine the CSS rules affecting their appearance.

For example, imagine that a heading has more spacing than expected. Instead of immediately editing the stylesheet, inspect the heading and review its computed styles.

You might discover that the spacing comes from a margin inherited through another CSS rule or from a conflicting selector.

You can also experiment with CSS properties directly inside DevTools.

If the card appears too wide, you can temporarily change its width or padding in the Styles panel.

The browser immediately displays the result, allowing you to compare different values without repeatedly editing and saving your stylesheet.

According to recent reports, however, these temporary changes do not automatically upgrade your original CSS files. Once you've identified the correct solution, apply it to your project source code.

For more detailed CSS debugging techniques, developers can also read SitePoint's guide on CSS Debugging and Optimization: Browser-based Developer Tools.

JavaScript errors can prevent interactive features from working correctly. A navigation menu might stop opening, a form might fail to submit, or a button might not trigger the expected action.

The Console panel helps developers investigate these problems.

For example, consider the following JavaScript:.

Industry observers note that if the page does not contain an element with the ID submitButton, the selected value will be null. Calling addEventListener() on that value causes an error.

You can prevent this particular matter by checking whether the element exists:.

The Console panel also allows developers to execute JavaScript expressions manually.

This returns the number of image elements currently present in the document.

You can use similar expressions to inspect elements, check values, and test small pieces of functionality.

Sometimes a JavaScript error is not immediately visible. A function may execute successfully but produce an unexpected result.

In such cases, the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools or the Debugger panel in Firefox can help.

Recent findings suggest that A breakpoint pauses JavaScript execution at a specific line. Developers can then inspect variable values, examine the call stack, and execute the code step by step.

If the application displays an incorrect total, you can place a breakpoint inside calculateTotal().

When the function executes, the browser pauses and allows you to inspect the values of price, quantity, and total.

This is more useful than repeatedly adding console.log() statements throughout a large application.

Breakpoints are particularly helpful when debugging complex functions, asynchronous operations, and event handlers.

A webpage may contain several resources, including images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, fonts, and API requests.

If one of these resources fails to load, part of the website may stop working correctly.

The Network panel provides information about requests made by the browser.

It displays request URLs, HTTP status codes, response sizes, loading times, and other useful details.

For example, the following table explains some common HTTP responses developers may encounter:.

It has been revealed that suppose an image is missing from a product page. Open the Network panel, reload the page, and filter the requests by images.

If the image returns a 404 response, check whether the file path is correct and whether the resource exists on the server.

The same process can help investigate failed API requests.

For example, if a frontend application requests product information from an API, the Network panel allows you to inspect the request method, response status, and returned data.

This helps developers distinguish between frontend problems and backend errors.

A website that looks correct on a desktop computer may not work properly on a smartphone.

Text can overflow, navigation menus can become difficult to use, and images may extend beyond their containers.

Browser DevTools include responsive design and device emulation features that allow developers to test different viewport sizes.

In Chrome, you can enable the device toolbar from the DevTools interface. Firefox provides a similar feature called Responsive Design Mode.

The desktop layout displays three columns, while smaller screens display one column.

You can test this behavior by changing the viewport width inside DevTools.

A useful responsive testing process includes:.

Checking common mobile and tablet widths.

Testing both portrait and landscape orientations.

Looking for horizontal scrolling.

Checking whether navigation remains usable.

Verifying that buttons and links are easy to interact with.

Device emulation is useful during development, but it does not completely replace testing on physical devices.

A website can have correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but still provide a poor experience if it loads slowly or performs unnecessary work.

The Performance panel helps developers investigate browser activity over time.

It can record page interactions and provide information about scripting, rendering, painting, and other browser operations.

Industry observers note that for example, a page might become unresponsive when a user opens a navigation menu. A performance recording can help identify whether a long-running JavaScript function is blocking the main thread.

Developers can also use tools such as Lighthouse to audit performance, accessibility, SEO, and other aspects of a webpage.

Instead of making random optimization changes, use the available measurements to identify the actual problem.

Some useful areas to investigate include:.

Unnecessary JavaScript execution.

Excessive layout recalculations.

Performance analysis should be repeated after making changes to determine whether the optimization actually improves the result.

These features are useful, but they can also introduce debugging challenges.

For example, an application might continue displaying outdated information because an old value remains stored in local storage.

The Application panel in Chrome DevTools allows developers to inspect and manage several types of browser storage.

Consider this simple JavaScript example:.

If the application behaves unexpectedly because of stored data, inspecting local storage can help identify the problem.

Be careful when clearing storage because doing so may remove authentication sessions, saved preferences, or other application data.

Knowing individual DevTools features is useful, but developers benefit even more from using them in a consistent order.

The following workflow can make troubleshooting more efficient:.

This process helps developers identify the cause of a problem before changing multiple parts of the application.

It also makes debugging easier when working with other developers because the glitch can be reproduced and explained using specific observations.

Browser developer tools are essential for modern web development. They help developers inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, analyze network requests, test responsive layouts, and investigate performance complications.

The most effective approach is to select the appropriate tool for the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Whether you're working on a small website or a complex web application, becoming familiar with DevTools can make your development workflow more efficient and help you build websites that are easier to maintain.

Sources indicate that rather than treating debugging as something that happens only after development, make it a regular part of your workflow. This allows you to identify problems earlier, verify your solutions, and deliver more reliable web experiences.

From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • In a recent development, previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota.
  • In a recent development, “At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

In a recent development, previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

In a recent development, “At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”.

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI.

Sources indicate that with the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:.

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

Sources indicate that when selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that on the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

According to recent reports, you’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

Industry observers note that you arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

You can try this experience today:.

Sources indicate that the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

MotorCity Casino Gains 15.6% as MGM and Greektown Slip in Detroit’s October Revenue

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier.
  • It has been revealed that motorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier.
  • Across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

It has been revealed that motorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

Across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

Sources indicate that MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

It has been revealed that the October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

Sources indicate that greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

Recent findings suggest that the citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

According to recent reports, retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

Industry observers note that motorCity also led the sportsbook results. It posted $928,607 in retail receipts. MGM followed at $746,215, with Hollywood Casino at Greektown close behind at $729,350.

The sportsbook activity generated $90,878 in state taxes. The casinos also sent $111,073 in sports wagering taxes to Detroit.

In a recent development, the city’s take from the casinos goes well beyond sports betting. In October, Detroit collected $13.4 million from the three properties, combining its share of gaming taxes with sums owed under each casino’s agreement with the city.

Native-speed vLLM transformers modeling backend

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures.
  • The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

Recent findings suggest that we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A major step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

This integration gets better now 🚀!

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:.

It has been revealed that running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:.

Sources indicate that *Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:.

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Recent findings suggest that retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

According to recent reports, an idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

Recent findings suggest that we'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

In a recent development, the client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:.

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:.

To tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only shows up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:.

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:.

In a recent development, two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

The draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:.

The fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:.

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

The tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

Instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:.

The UPDATE in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Industry observers note that set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

Industry observers note that once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still says in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:.

releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

According to recent reports, the route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:.

The server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a latest key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:.

Industry observers note that the catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

In a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a upcoming key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

Keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but says it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:.

In a recent development, run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a fresh request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:.

Sources indicate that the second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:.

To see the concurrent case, add await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:.

In a recent development, one request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

In a recent development, this design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:.

According to recent reports, idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

With one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

Recent findings suggest that the same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.
